description: Terminal page -- an integrated multi-page, multi-tab PTY terminal with workflow generation, session transcript browsing, terminal output analysis, findings tracking, and concurrent session file conflict detection. Users can create multiple terminal pages (e.g., Development, Testing, Monitoring), each with its own independent zone layout, terminals, and saved configurations. Within each page, users execute shell commands in multiple concurrent terminal sessions organized in configurable zone layouts. The terminal supports session persistence across restarts (Claude Code session IDs are saved and auto-resumed), zone profiles that capture session assignments, shell integration for structured command history, keyboard shortcuts for efficient tab management, and an advisory file registry that auto-detects file conflicts across sessions, and plan implementation workflow execution from both the UI (Implement/Verify buttons) and CLI (run-plan-implementation.ts script).

groups.name: Multi-Tab Terminal Sessions
groups.description: Users work with multiple concurrent terminal sessions organized as tabs. Each tab is an independent PTY session with its own shell, working directory, command history, and scrollback buffer. Users can create new tabs (Ctrl+Shift+T), close tabs (Ctrl+Shift+W), cycle between tabs (Ctrl+Tab), and rename tabs for better organization. Tabs auto-rename from the first command entered. On mount, the terminal attempts to reconnect to existing Rust PTY sessions from previous page visits, preserving shell state across navigation. When all tabs are closed, a helpful empty state guides users on how to create a new terminal.

assertions.description: Users can see and interact with a tab bar showing all open terminal sessions, with the active tab visually distinguished from inactive ones
Users can create new terminal sessions either by clicking the + button in the tab bar or pressing Ctrl+Shift+T, immediately getting a fresh shell prompt
When no terminal tabs are open, users see a helpful message explaining how to create a new terminal with the Ctrl+Shift+T shortcut or the + button
Users can manage terminal tabs entirely via keyboard shortcuts: Ctrl+Shift+T to create, Ctrl+Shift+W to close, Ctrl+Tab to cycle forward, and Ctrl+Shift+Tab to cycle backward

groups.name: Terminal Action Bar
groups.description: Above the terminal area, an action bar provides quick access to terminal-augmented features: toggling the transcript session sidebar, triggering AI-powered analysis of terminal output, generating workflows from the latest Claude Code session, refreshing the plan file, and toggling the findings panel. The action bar adapts its button states based on context -- showing loading spinners during generation or analysis, indicating the active findings count, and highlighting the active panel mode. This bar transforms the terminal from a simple shell into an intelligent development workbench.

assertions.description: Users can toggle the transcript session sidebar to browse and resume previous Claude Code sessions directly from the terminal page
Users can generate a workflow from the latest Claude Code session transcript, transforming ad-hoc terminal work into a repeatable automated workflow
Users can run AI-powered analysis on terminal output with multiple analysis types: session summary, architecture review, change impact, progress tracking, and cross-tab analysis
Users can toggle the findings panel to see errors, warnings, and issues automatically detected from terminal output in real-time, with a badge showing the active findings count

groups.name: Claude Code Session Transcripts
groups.description: The left sidebar shows a list of Claude Code session transcripts from the local machine. Users can browse past sessions, view the full conversation transcript in a right-side content panel, and resume sessions in a new terminal tab. Session resumption creates a new tab, sets the working directory, and sends the 'claude --resume' command with the correct config directory. The transcript panel supports generating workflows from session content and generating-and-running workflows in a single action for rapid automation creation.

assertions.description: Users can browse a list of past Claude Code sessions in the sidebar, seeing session identifiers and project paths to find the session they want to review or resume
Users can click a session to view its full conversation transcript in a right-side panel, reading the complete AI conversation history including tool calls and responses
Users can resume a previous Claude Code session in a new terminal tab, continuing the conversation exactly where it left off with the correct project context and config directory
Users can generate a reusable workflow from a session transcript, converting a one-off Claude Code conversation into an automated workflow that can be saved, edited, and re-run

groups.name: Workflow Generation and Preview
groups.description: When a workflow is generated (from a session transcript, command history, or findings), a preview panel opens on the right side showing the full workflow structure. Users can review the generated workflow's phases and steps, then choose to execute it immediately, save it to the workflow library for later use, edit it in the Workflow Builder for refinement, or regenerate it with different parameters. The panel shows loading state during generation and error messages if generation fails. This workflow enables a rapid 'do it once in the terminal, then automate it' development pattern.
groups._setupNote: This group requires a workflow to have been generated first (via Sessions > select session > Generate). The deterministic buildSpecWorkflow path cannot reliably trigger generation; the AI path handles this via preconditions.

assertions.description: After generating a workflow, users see a preview panel showing the complete workflow structure with all phases and steps before deciding what to do with it
Users can execute the generated workflow immediately from the preview panel, which sends it to the runner and navigates to the Active Dashboard for monitoring
Users can save the generated workflow to the library for later use, making it available on the Execute page and in the Workflow Builder
Users can open the generated workflow in the Workflow Builder for manual refinement of steps, phases, and settings before saving or executing

groups.name: Real-Time Findings Detection
groups.description: The terminal automatically analyzes output in real time to detect errors, warnings, test failures, and other notable findings. These are tracked per-session and displayed in a dedicated findings panel on the right side. Users can respond to findings (sending text back to the terminal), fix findings by spawning a new Claude Code session with the finding context pre-loaded, or batch-generate a workflow from multiple unresolved findings. The findings count badge on the action bar updates live as new issues are detected, keeping users aware of problems without interrupting their terminal workflow.

assertions.description: Users can view all detected findings in a dedicated panel, seeing each finding's severity, category, title, description, and relevant code context
Users can fix a finding by spawning a new terminal tab with Claude Code pre-loaded with the finding context, immediately beginning an AI-assisted fix session
Users can batch-generate a workflow from multiple unresolved findings, creating an automated fix pipeline that addresses all detected issues systematically
Users can respond to a finding by sending text directly to the active terminal, useful for answering questions or providing input that the terminal process is waiting for

groups.name: AI-Powered Terminal Analysis
groups.description: The terminal integrates AI analysis capabilities that process terminal scrollback, command history, and plan files to produce structured insights. Analysis types include: session summary (what happened in this terminal session), architecture review (system structure from plan files or terminal context), change impact (what files and systems were affected), progress tracking (how far along is the development plan), cross-tab analysis (correlating activity across multiple terminal sessions), and page architecture (analyzing the runner's own frontend). Analysis results appear in a dedicated panel with structured canvas-style panels. This transforms raw terminal output into actionable development intelligence.

assertions.description: Users can view analysis results in a dedicated right-side panel showing structured AI-generated insights about their terminal activity
Users can choose from multiple analysis types including session summary, architecture review, change impact, progress tracking, and cross-tab analysis to get the specific insight they need
During analysis, users see a loading indicator so they know the AI is processing their terminal output and can wait for results rather than re-triggering

groups.name: File Conflict Detection Banner
groups.description: The Terminal page includes an advisory file conflict detection system that tracks which files are under active development by concurrent sessions (workflows and AI terminal sessions). When multiple sessions edit the same file, a warning banner appears below the notification bar showing conflicting files and which sessions hold them. Real-time toast alerts appear when a new conflict is detected (e.g., session B starts editing a file that session A already registered). The banner is collapsible â€” a summary line shows the count of conflicting files, and expanding reveals the full list with file paths and session names. The system auto-registers files when Claude Code uses Edit or Write tools, polls the runner's file registry API every 30 seconds, and listens for real-time Tauri events. The banner uses warning amber (#e0af68) coloring consistent with the 'needs-input' status style.

assertions.description: When no files are under concurrent development (no file registry conflicts), the FileConflictBanner component renders nothing â€” no banner, no summary line, no empty state. The banner only appears when there are active conflicts.
assertions.precondition: No files are registered by multiple sessions in the file registry (GET /file-registry/info returns entries with unique holder_task_run_id per file_path)

assertions.description: When files are under concurrent development, a collapsible summary line appears showing '{N} file(s) under concurrent development' with a FileWarning icon in amber (#e0af68) and a chevron toggle. The text uses 'file' (singular) when N=1 and 'files' (plural) when N>1.
assertions.precondition: At least one file is registered by two or more distinct sessions in the file registry

assertions.description: Clicking the summary line toggles an expanded view showing each conflicting file path (in monospace font, color #a9b1d6 at 90% opacity) and the session names holding that file (in parentheses, color #a9b1d6 at 50% opacity, comma-separated). Each file is preceded by a dash in amber at 60% opacity.
assertions.precondition: File conflict banner is visible with at least one conflict

assertions.description: When a real-time 'file-conflict-detected' Tauri event fires (triggered when a session edits a file already held by another session), a toast-style alert appears at the top of the banner showing 'Conflict: {file_path} is also being edited by {holder_name}' with an AlertTriangle icon in amber. The alert has a dismiss X button and auto-dismisses after 10 seconds. Only the most recent alert is shown; new alerts replace previous ones.
assertions.precondition: A file-conflict-detected event has been emitted by the runner within the last 10 seconds

assertions.description: The conflict banner uses a consistent amber warning theme: text color #e0af68 at 80% opacity for the summary, border-bottom with #e0af68 at 20% opacity, and the FileWarning icon at full #e0af68. The toast alert uses background #e0af68 at 15% opacity with text at full #e0af68 and a border-bottom at 20% opacity. This matches the 'needs-input' status dot color used elsewhere in the Terminal page.
assertions.precondition: File conflict banner is visible

groups.name: Per-Session File Conflict Indicators
groups.description: Each session card in the SessionManagerPanel sidebar displays a file conflict warning icon when that session has files overlapping with other active sessions. The indicator shows a FileWarning icon in amber (#e0af68) with a numeric count badge showing how many conflicting files that session has. The count is derived from the file registry: for each file registered by this session, if any OTHER session also has that file registered, it counts as a conflict. The tooltip shows '{N} file(s) shared with other sessions'. Sessions with zero conflicts show no indicator. The conflict count is computed by the useFileConflicts hook's sessionConflictCounts Map, keyed by session task_run_id.

assertions.description: When a session has fileConflictCount > 0, its SessionCard displays a FileWarning icon (w-3 h-3, color #e0af68) followed by the numeric count in 9px text at #e0af68 with 80% opacity. The icon and count are wrapped in a span with a title tooltip reading '{N} file(s) shared with other sessions' (using singular 'file' for count=1). The indicator appears between the session label badges and the pin icon in the card's first row.
assertions.precondition: At least one session has files overlapping with another session in the file registry

assertions.description: When a session has fileConflictCount === 0 (no file conflicts with other sessions), no FileWarning icon or count badge is rendered on its SessionCard. The indicator is completely absent, not just hidden or zeroed out.

target.label: Absent conflict indicator on non-conflicting session

assertions.precondition: The session has no files overlapping with other sessions

assertions.description: The numeric count shown on each session card accurately reflects the number of distinct files that session shares with at least one other session. For example, if session A edits files X, Y, Z and session B also edits files Y, Z, then session A's indicator shows '2' (files Y and Z are shared) and session B's indicator also shows '2'. The count updates when the file registry is refreshed (every 30 seconds or on real-time conflict events).
assertions.precondition: Multiple sessions are actively editing files with at least some overlap

assertions.description: When a new file-conflict-detected Tauri event fires, the useFileConflicts hook immediately refreshes the file registry from GET /file-registry/info, which updates the sessionConflictCounts Map, causing affected SessionCards to re-render with updated conflict counts. This means users see conflict indicators appear within seconds of another session editing a shared file, not just at the 30-second poll interval.
assertions.precondition: A file-conflict-detected event was just emitted

groups.name: Multiple Terminal Pages
groups.description: Users can create multiple independent terminal pages, each with its own zone layout, terminals, labels, and saved configurations. A page tab bar at the top of the terminal area shows all pages. Clicking a page tab switches to that page by unmounting the current TerminalPage and remounting a new one connected to that page's PTY sessions. Each page's state (zone layout, labels, notes, pins, zone profiles, workspaces) is stored in page-namespaced localStorage keys. The default page uses un-prefixed keys for backward compatibility. PTY sessions are tagged with a page_id in the Rust backend, so each page only sees its own terminals.

assertions.description: A page tab bar is always visible above the terminal area, showing one button per page with the page name. The active page tab has a distinct background color (bg-[#2a2d3d]) while inactive tabs are muted (text-[#565f89]). Each tab is a button element with role='tab' and aria-selected indicating the active state.

A '+' button is present in the page tab bar allowing users to create a new terminal page. Clicking it creates a page named 'Page N' (where N is the next sequential number), switches to that page, and the new page starts with a single fresh terminal.

Switching between pages preserves each page's terminals independently. If page A has 4 terminals and page B has 1, switching from A to B shows 1 terminal, and switching back to A shows 4 terminals. PTY processes stay alive during switches â€” they are filtered by page_id in the Rust backend.
assertions.precondition: At least two pages exist with different numbers of terminals

assertions.description: Double-clicking a page tab enters inline rename mode, replacing the tab label with a text input pre-filled with the current name. Pressing Enter commits the rename, Escape cancels. The input has a blue border (border-[#7aa2f7]) and is auto-focused with text selected.

Each page tab (when there are 2+ pages) shows a close button on hover. Clicking it removes the page, closes all its PTY sessions via terminal_close, cleans up namespaced localStorage keys, and switches to another page. The last remaining page cannot be closed.
assertions.precondition: At least two pages exist

assertions.description: Page configurations persist across runner restarts. After restarting, all previously created pages appear in the tab bar with their original names, and each page reconnects to its own PTY sessions (filtered by page_id).
assertions.precondition: Runner was restarted after pages were created

assertions.description: During page switch, a loading spinner with 'Loading terminals...' text is shown while the new page initializes and reconnects to its PTY sessions. The spinner is a border-spinning animation in primary blue (border-[#7aa2f7]).
assertions.precondition: User just switched to a different page

groups.name: Session Persistence & Auto-Resume
groups.description: Claude Code session IDs are persisted alongside terminal tab configurations. When the runner restarts and reconnects to existing PTY sessions, saved claudeSessionId values are merged back into the reconnected tabs and the sessions are auto-resumed with 'claude --resume <id>'. This ensures that Claude Code sessions survive runner restarts without manual intervention. The saved layout includes zone assignments, labels, notes, pins, and Claude session IDs per tab.

assertions.description: After a runner restart, Claude Code sessions that were running before the restart are automatically resumed in their original terminal zones. The resume command 'claude --resume <sessionId>' is sent to each terminal that had an active Claude session. Session IDs are validated against a safe character set before being written to the terminal.
assertions.precondition: Runner was restarted after Claude sessions were running in terminal zones

assertions.description: Zone labels, notes, and pin states are restored after reconnection. If zone 0 was labeled 'Backend' with pinned state, after restart it still shows 'Backend' and remains pinned.
assertions.precondition: Zones had labels/notes/pins before runner restart

assertions.description: Zone profiles (save/load configurations via the FolderOpen dropdown) capture Claude session IDs alongside layout, labels, notes, and pins. The profile display shows a session count badge (e.g., '3 sessions') in blue text when sessions are included. Loading a profile with sessions resumes those Claude sessions into the appropriate zones.

The zone profile save flow has discoverable interactive elements: a 'Save current configuration' button (id=zone-profile-save-current) that reveals a text input (id=zone-profile-name-input) for the profile name, and a save confirmation button (id=zone-profile-save-btn). The input accepts up to 30 characters.
assertions.precondition: Zone profiles dropdown is open

groups.name: Per-Page Storage Isolation
groups.description: Each terminal page has isolated storage for its configuration. Zone layouts, session persistence, zone profiles, workspaces, zone labels/notes/pins, and grid column/row ratios are all namespaced by pageId. The default page uses un-prefixed keys (backward compatible), while non-default pages use 'page:{pageId}:' prefixed keys. This ensures that creating a zone profile on page A does not appear when viewing page B's profiles.

assertions.description: Zone profiles saved on one page are not visible on another page. If page A has a profile 'Dev Setup' and the user switches to page B and opens the zone profiles dropdown, 'Dev Setup' should not appear â€” page B has its own independent profile list.
assertions.precondition: Multiple pages exist, at least one has saved profiles

assertions.description: Zone layout configurations (quad, six-pack, etc.) are independent per page. Changing page A to a 'six-pack' layout does not affect page B's layout, which remains at its own setting (e.g., 'quad').

target.label: Page tabs for layout isolation check

assertions.precondition: Multiple pages with different layouts

assertions.description: Zone labels and notes are independent per page. Setting zone 0's label to 'Backend' on page A does not affect zone 0's label on page B.

target.label: Page tabs for label isolation check

assertions.precondition: Multiple pages with zone labels configured

groups.name: Plan Implementation Workflow
groups.description: Users can build and execute multi-stage plan implementation workflows directly from the Terminal page. Two entry points exist: (1) from a transcript panel, select messages containing a plan and click Implement to build a workflow with implement/review/next-steps stages per phase, or (2) from the status bar, click Implement next to a detected plan file. The Implement button (amber, Rocket icon) is the primary action; the Verify button (gray, ListChecks icon) builds a lighter verification-only workflow. Both parse the plan markdown into phases and tasks, build a multi-stage UnifiedWorkflow, and show it in the workflow preview panel for execution.

assertions.description: When viewing a transcript, an Implement button (amber/gold, Rocket icon) appears in the footer alongside Generate and Run. Clicking it extracts plan content from selected messages, parses phases and tasks, builds a plan implementation workflow (3 stages per phase: implement, review, next-steps), and shows it in the workflow preview panel.

target.label: Implement plan button in transcript panel

assertions.precondition: Transcript panel is open with messages selected

assertions.description: A secondary Verify button (gray, ListChecks icon) appears next to Implement in the transcript footer. It builds a lighter verification-only plan workflow (1 stage per phase with deterministic checks) instead of the full implement/review/next-steps workflow.

target.label: Verify plan button in transcript panel

assertions.precondition: Transcript panel is open with messages selected

assertions.description: When a plan file (PLAN*.md, TODO*.md, NOTES*.md, ROADMAP*.md) is detected in the workspace, the status bar shows the filename in green with an Implement button (amber, Rocket icon) next to it. Clicking Implement parses the file content, builds a plan implementation workflow, and shows the preview panel.

target.label: Implement plan from file button in status bar

assertions.precondition: A plan file is detected in the workspace (plan filename badge visible in status bar)

assertions.description: A secondary Verify button (gray, ListChecks icon) appears next to Implement in the status bar plan file area. It builds the lighter verification-only workflow from the plan file.

target.label: Verify plan from file button in status bar

assertions.precondition: A plan file is detected in the workspace

assertions.description: The plan implementation workflow generated by the Implement button creates 3 stages per plan phase (Implement, Review, Next Steps) plus a final Commit stage. Each stage has its own agentic prompt and compile-check verification step. The workflow preview panel should show all stages with names like 'Phase 1: Implement -- [name]', 'Phase 1: Review -- [name]', 'Phase 1: Next Steps -- [name]'.

target.label: Plan implementation workflow in preview panel

assertions.precondition: A plan implementation workflow has been built and is shown in the preview panel

assertions.description: A refresh button (circular arrow icon) in the status bar plan file area reloads the plan file from disk. When no plan file is found, the status bar shows 'no plan' text instead of a filename. After clicking refresh, if a plan file is now present, the filename appears and the Implement/Verify buttons become visible.

groups.name: Plan Implementation CLI Script
groups.description: A standalone CLI script (scripts/run-plan-implementation.ts) allows launching plan implementation workflows from any Claude Code session without the runner UI. The script parses markdown plan files, builds the same multi-stage workflow as the UI Implement button, and POSTs it to the runner execute-inline endpoint. It supports --dry-run for inspection and --follow for streaming progress.

assertions.description: The script correctly parses markdown plans with numbered headings (### 1. Name) as phases and sub-items (numbered lists, bullets) as tasks. Non-actionable sections (Context, Goal, Reference, Validation, Implementation Order) are skipped.

Running the script with a plan file POSTs the generated workflow to /unified-workflows/execute-inline on the target runner port. The endpoint returns HTTP 200 and the workflow starts executing asynchronously.
The --follow flag polls /task-runs/{id}/workflow-state every 5 seconds and streams phase transitions, iteration counts, and pass/fail status to stderr until completion.

states.name: Loading Terminals
states.description: Transient state shown while the TerminalPage initializes and reconnects to existing PTY sessions. Displays a spinner and 'Loading terminals...' text on a blank background.

states.name: No Terminals Open
states.description: Shown when all terminal tabs have been closed. Displays a message guiding users to create a new terminal via Ctrl+Shift+T or the + button. The tab bar, status bar, and page tab bar remain visible.

states.name: Active Terminal Workspace
states.description: The primary state of the terminal page. Shows the tab bar with open terminal sessions, a zone grid with one or more terminal instances, the zone status bar with action buttons (Sessions, Generate, Analyze, Findings), the page tab bar, and optional file conflict banner. The right panel and session sidebar are hidden.

states.name: Sessions Sidebar Open
states.description: The left sidebar is visible showing the session manager panel with a list of active terminal sessions and Claude Code transcript sessions. Users can browse, resume, and select sessions from this panel. The terminal zone grid shrinks to accommodate the sidebar.

states.name: Transcript Panel Open
states.description: The right panel shows a Claude Code session transcript with the full conversation history. Footer buttons allow generating a workflow (Generate), generating and running (Run), implementing a plan (Implement), verifying a plan (Verify), or resuming the session in a terminal (Resume).

states.name: Workflow Preview Panel
states.description: The right panel shows a generated workflow with its phases and steps. Users can execute the workflow, save it to the library, edit it in the Workflow Builder, or regenerate it. Shown after generating a workflow from a session transcript, findings, or plan file.

states.name: Analysis Panel Open
states.description: The right panel shows AI-generated analysis results in structured canvas-style panels. Analysis types include session summary, architecture review, change impact, progress tracking, and cross-tab analysis. Shows a loading indicator during analysis.

states.name: Findings Panel Open
states.description: The right panel shows real-time detected findings (errors, warnings, test failures) from terminal output. Each finding has Fix, Respond, and Generate Workflow actions. The panel shows both active and historical findings.

states.name: Keyboard Shortcuts Overlay
states.description: A modal overlay displaying all available keyboard shortcuts for terminal management, zone navigation, batch operations, and more. Appears on top of the terminal workspace.

states.name: Command Palette
states.description: A modal command palette overlay allowing users to search and execute commands for zone management, batch operations, snapshot comparison, and more. Opened via Ctrl+Shift+P.
